content: 1. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have tuberculosis (TB) disease, based on appropriate clinical evaluation or national guidelines, should receive TB preventive treatment as part of a comprehensive HIV care package. This includes individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART), pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression or the availability of TB infection testing. 2. Infants under 12 months of age living with HIV who have been in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have active TB, based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines, should receive TB preventive treatment. 3. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV who are unlikely to have TB disease, based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines, should be offered TB preventive treatment as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention and care package, especially in settings with high TB transmission, regardless of TB contact history. 4. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may receive TB preventive treatment. 5. Children under 5 years of age who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB, based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines, should be given TB preventive treatment, even if latent TB infection (LTBI) testing is unavailable. 6. Children aged 5 years or older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB, based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines, may be given TB preventive treatment. 7. People initiating anti-tumor necrosis factor treatment, receiving dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplantation, or diagnosed with silicosis should be systematically tested and treated for TB infection. 8. Systematic testing and treatment for TB infection may be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. 9. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment, regardless of ART status. Those with symptoms should be evaluated for TB and other diseases, and if TB is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. 10. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, chest X-rays may be used to screen for TB disease. 11. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, C-reactive protein levels above 5 mg/L may be used to screen for TB disease. 12. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests may be used to screen for TB disease. 13. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, current cough, or have a history of contact with a person with TB should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing these symptoms. If TB is excluded, they should be offered TB preventive treatment, regardless of age. 14. Among HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other at-risk groups, the absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings may be used to rule out TB disease before initiating TB preventive treatment. 15. Among individuals aged 15 years or older in populations where TB screening is recommended, systematic screening for TB disease may involve symptom screening, chest X-rays, or molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests, alone or in combination. 16. Among individuals under 15 years of age who are close contacts of a person with TB, systematic screening for TB disease should include symptom screening (cough, fever, or poor weight gain), chest radiography, or both. 17. Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for TB infection. 18. Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBST) may also be used to test for TB infection. 19. Recommended TB preventive treatment regimens, regardless of HIV status, include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. 20. Alternative TB preventive treatment regimens, regardless of HIV status, include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin. 21. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). 22. For contacts exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB, 6 months of daily levofloxacin should be used as TB preventive treatment.
